chunks: Power sequencing and why it matters. The question: What is power sequencing? Why is it important?
Power sequencing means controlling the order and timing in which a board's supply voltages (called rails) turn on, and turn off.
Many chips need several rails, such as one for the core and one for the pins. If the rails come up in the wrong order, the chip can misbehave or be damaged.
Sequencing is the plan that prevents that.
Think of getting dressed. Socks go on before shoes. Do it the other way around and the job is awkward, even if both items end up on your feet. Chips are the same: order matters.
Some chips do not care; others list the required order in their datasheet.
The simplest robust sequence is a chain: each rail's power-good enables the next, and reset is released only after the last rail has been good for a hold time.
Because the chain is threshold-based, it adapts automatically to slow start-ups, load and temperature.
Rail: one supply voltage line on a board, such as 1. 0 volts or 3. 3 volts.
Back-powering: current flowing into an unpowered chip through a driven pin and the chip's protection diodes, which partly powers it in an unplanned state.
Power-good: a signal from a regulator that says its output is ready and within range.
Soft-start: a controlled slow rise of a rail, to limit the surge of current that charges the capacitors. Reset: holding a chip inactive until its rails and clock are stable.
Chip A runs from a 3. 3 volts rail that is already up, and it drives a signal line high. Chip B shares that line, but its own 3. 3 volts rail is still off.
The line pushes current backward through a protection diode (a one-way valve for current) built into B's pin, into B's off rail, partly powering B in a state nobody designed.
The fix is sequencing. Bring B's rail up first, or hold A in reset until B's power-good signal says B is ready.
Ramp speed matters too: charging a 1 mF capacitor to 1 volts in 1 milliseconds takes 1 amps of current. That is the whole idea: order and ramp both matter.
"Power sequencing is controlling the order, timing and ramp of the rails on a multi-rail board, up and down.

It matters because chips have rules between their rails: ESD diodes back-power an unpowered rail, I/O above core can cause latch-up or contention, resets must release only when everything is stable, and analog and memory rails have ordering.
It also matters for power integrity: starting every regulator at once charges all the capacitance together, an inrush of C dV over dt that can trip limits.
You use power-good chaining, sequencers or a PMIC, and verify on a scope."
